title: Anthropo
description: Anthropomorphic cinematography stages an object or animal as a performer: human scale in the frame, a gesture, an eyeline, reaction shots, as if the inanimate had a will. The camera does not need a face so much as an actor's grammar.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: A red balloon waits, follows, sulks. A robot tilts its head at a trash cube.
The object is not a prop in a still life. It is covered like a person: singles, looks, pauses.
Will is implied by blocking and eyeline, not by a drawn smile unless the story needs one. Use it to give a thing agency: a balloon, a machine, a relic, an animal shot as a colleague.

The rest of the scene should treat it as a presence. It is the wrong tool when you simply shoot an object from its own optical position (that is object POV) or when a tableau arranges bodies as a picture.
Anthropo is performance coverage of a nonhuman. Object POV is a camera mount.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Assign an eyeline height. Cover the object with the same sizes you would give an actor: wide for entrance, medium for dialogue, close for reaction.
Let humans look at it as a partner. Puppet, wire, or animation can supply gesture.
Prompt: an object or animal given human scale, gesture, or eyeline, the inanimate performing, not a POV from inside the object.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: A balloon at head height, held in a single, a child looking to it as if it might answer. Do not bolt the camera to the balloon and call that anthropo.
That is object POV.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: Object POV puts the camera in the object's position. Anthropo looks at the object as an actor.
Tableau freezes people into a composed picture. Anthropo keeps a will in motion.
Macro can isolate an object as texture without giving it an eyeline.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: The Red Balloon covers a balloon as a companion, with waits and follows that belong to a performer. WALL-E plays a machine with human gesture and eyeline without needing a human face.
Those are coverage choices, not mascots to copy.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: Wrong cousin: object POV, a cute sticker face, or a still-life insert. Tell: the camera is mounted in the object, or the object sits as a prop with no eyeline.
Fix: assign a look, a height, and reaction coverage. Let others treat it as a partner.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is anthropo in film?
Staging and covering an object or animal as if it were a performer: scale, gesture, eyeline, reactions. Agency is in the blocking, not necessarily in a painted face.
Anthropo vs object POV
Object POV is the camera from the thing's position. Anthropo is the camera looking at the thing as an actor. One is a mount. The other is a performance.
When should I use anthropo?
When a nonhuman should have a will in the scene. Do not use it for a mere product insert or for a true POV from inside the object.
How do I prompt anthropo for AI image or video?
Specify human scale, a clear eyeline, gesture, and coverage as if the object were a player. Forbid interior POV unless you want that cousin.
